title: Book Thirteen (1812) — Chapter 15
paragraphs: In the early days of October, another envoy came to Kutuzov with a letter from Napoleon proposing peace, falsely dated from Moscow, though Napoleon was already not far from Kutuzov on the old Kaluga road. Kutuzov replied as he had to Lauriston's earlier letter, saying there could be no question of peace.

Soon after, a report came in from Dorokhov's guerrilla detachment, operating to the left of Tarutino, that troops from Broussier's division had been spotted at Forminsk and, being separated from the main French army, could easily be destroyed. The soldiers and officers again demanded action. Generals on the staff, emboldened by the easy victory at Tarutino, urged Kutuzov to follow Dorokhov's suggestion. Kutuzov didn't think any offensive was necessary. The result was an inevitable compromise: a small detachment was sent to Forminsk to attack Broussier.

By a strange coincidence, this task—which turned out to be one of the most difficult and important of the campaign—was given to Dokhturov, that same modest little Dokhturov whom no one has ever described drawing up battle plans, charging in front of regiments, or showering decorations on batteries, and who was considered and spoken of as indecisive and lacking insight. Yet we find him in command at the most critical position in every engagement of the Russo-French wars from Austerlitz to 1813. At Austerlitz he was the last to hold the Augezd dam, rallying regiments and saving what he could when everyone was fleeing and not a single general remained in the rear guard. Ill with fever, he went to Smolensk with twenty thousand men to defend it against Napoleon's entire army. At the Malakhov Gate in Smolensk, he had barely dozed off in a bout of fever before being woken by the bombardment—and Smolensk held out all day. At Borodino, when Bagration was killed and nine-tenths of the men on the left flank had fallen and the full force of French artillery was directed there, the man sent to that spot was this same 'irresolute and unperceptive' Dokhturov—Kutuzov rushing to correct a mistake he'd made by first sending someone else. And the quiet little Dokhturov rode there, and Borodino became the greatest glory of the Russian army. Many heroes of that time have been celebrated in verse and prose, but about Dokhturov, scarcely a word has been said.

It was Dokhturov again who was sent to Forminsk and from there to Malo-Yaroslavets—the site of the last battle with the French, where the obvious disintegration of the French army began. We hear about many geniuses and heroes of that campaign, but about Dokhturov, nothing or almost nothing, and even that is said doubtfully. This silence about Dokhturov is the clearest proof of his merit.

It's natural for someone who doesn't understand how a machine works to assume that a wood shaving that has accidentally fallen into it and is bouncing around, interfering with its operation, must be its most important part. Someone who doesn't understand the machine's construction can't grasp that the small connecting cog, turning quietly, is one of the most essential parts—not the shaving that merely damages and hinders it.

On October tenth, Dokhturov had gotten halfway to Forminsk and stopped at the village of Aristovo, faithfully preparing to carry out his orders. Then the entire French army—having lurched convulsively toward Murat's position as if to give battle—suddenly and for no apparent reason veered left onto the new Kaluga road and began pouring into Forminsk, where previously only Broussier had been. At that point, Dokhturov had under his command, besides Dorokhov's detachment, the two small guerrilla bands of Figner and Seslavin.

On the evening of October eleventh, Seslavin arrived at Aristovo headquarters with a captured French guardsman. The prisoner said the troops entering Forminsk that day were the vanguard of the entire army—Napoleon was there, and the whole army had left Moscow four days earlier. That same evening, a house servant from Borovsk said he'd seen an enormous army entering the town. Cossacks from Dokhturov's detachment reported sighting the French Guards marching toward Borovsk. From all these reports, it was clear that where they had expected to find a single division, they now faced the entire French army, marching from Moscow in an unexpected direction along the Kaluga road. Dokhturov was unwilling to act, as it was no longer clear what he should do. He'd been ordered to attack Forminsk, but at that time only Broussier had been there—now the whole French army was there. Ermolov wanted to act on his own judgment, but Dokhturov insisted on getting instructions from Kutuzov. So it was decided to send a dispatch to the staff.

For this mission, they chose a capable officer named Bolkhovitinov, who was to explain the situation verbally as well as deliver a written report. Toward midnight, Bolkhovitinov received the dispatch and verbal instructions and galloped off to General Staff headquarters, accompanied by a Cossack with spare horses.
